hints: Think about what can change the stored energy of a gas - heating it and squeezing or letting it expand are two different routes.
The + sign means energy is going into the system, so link +q to heating the system and +w to compressing the system by an outside force.
walkthrough:
**What Delta U Means**
Internal energy $U$ of an ideal gas is the total kinetic energy of its molecules. It only goes up if extra energy is put into the system from outside.

**Two Ways To Add Energy**
You can add energy by heating, so $+q$ is energy in by thermal transfer to the system. You can also add energy by pushing a piston in, so $+w$ is energy in by work done on the system. Both make $\Delta U$ positive: $$\Delta U = (+q) + (+w)$$
Final answer: +q is the thermal energy transferred to the system. +w is the work done on the system.

hints: Look closely at the line A to B in Fig. 2.1 - check what happens to $p$ while $V$ increases, and note the start and finish values of $V$.
walkthrough:
**Spot Constant Pressure Expansion**
From A to B the pressure stays at $p = 2.6 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$ while volume grows. For constant pressure, the magnitude of work is pressure times volume change.

**Put In The Numbers**
$$W = p\Delta V$$ $$W = 2.6 \times 10^5 \times (3.8 \times 10^{-3} - 2.3 \times 10^{-3})$$ $$W = 2.6 \times 10^5 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 390\text{ J}$$ This is work done by the gas as it expands, so work done on the gas would be $-390\text{ J}$.

hints: After one full cycle A to B to C to A, compare the final pressure and volume with the starting pressure and volume.
Recall what controls the internal energy of a fixed mass of ideal gas, and what that implies if the start and end states are identical.
walkthrough:
**A Cycle Returns To Start**
A to B to C to A ends exactly where it began at A, so $p$ and $V$ are the same as at the start. From $pV = nRT$, the temperature $T$ must also be the same.

**Internal Energy Follows Temperature**
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. Same temperature means same internal energy, so over one complete cycle: $$\Delta U_{total} = 0$$
Final answer: No total change in internal energy. The gas returns to its original state so returns to its original temperature, and $U$ depends only on temperature.

hints: Start with A to B - you know heat in is 1370 J and the gas expands, so decide the sign of $w$ for work done on the gas.
For B to C no heat flows, so think about how $q$, $w$ and $\Delta U$ must be related when $q = 0$.
For C to A the volume does not change, so consider what that tells you about work done.
Use the fact that the three $\Delta U$ values must add to zero for the whole cycle to find the missing C to A change.
walkthrough:
**A to B - Heated Expansion**
Heat to gas $q = +1370\text{ J}$. Gas expands and does $390\text{ J}$ of work, so work done on gas is negative: $w = -390\text{ J}$. First law gives: $$\Delta U = q + w = 1370 - 390 = +980\text{ J}$$

**B to C - Adiabatic Compression**
No thermal transfer so $q = 0$. Work done on gas $w = +550\text{ J}$. Then: $$\Delta U = 0 + 550 = +550\text{ J}$$ Internal energy rises because work is done on the gas.

**C to A - Constant Volume Cooling**
Volume stays at $2.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$, so no work is done: $w = 0$. Let the unknown be $\Delta U_{CA}$. For a cycle total $\Delta U = 0$: $$980 + 550 + \Delta U_{CA} = 0$$ $$\Delta U_{CA} = -1530\text{ J}$$

**Find Heat For C to A**
Apply $\Delta U = q + w$ with $w = 0$: $$-1530 = q + 0$$ $$q = -1530\text{ J}$$ Negative means thermal energy leaves the gas as it is cooled at constant volume back to A.

Final answer: A to B: $q = +1370\text{ J}$, $w = -390\text{ J}$, $\Delta U = +980\text{ J}$. B to C: $q = 0$, $w = +550\text{ J}$, $\Delta U = +550\text{ J}$. C to A: $q = -1530\text{ J}$, $w = 0$, $\Delta U = -1530\text{ J}$.
